fullName: Polarization Modulation Spectroscopy: polarized hard X-rays for magnetism at extreme pressure, cold and field

status2026.detail: Operational and accepting general users, with on-site and remote access (APS beamline directory, read 2026-10-08). First light came in late 2024 / early 2025 after the 2023–24 installation (APS News, Jun 2026; APS-U updates, Sep and Oct 2024). The first users, a University of Wisconsin team studying flexomagnetism, came in the 2025-1 run (Jan–May 2025), while the beamline was still described as under commissioning in March 2025 (APS News, Jun 2025; APS News, Mar 2025). By August 2025 POLAR was no longer among the feature beamlines awaiting first experiments, and its lead engineer describes 'experiments across three instrument stations' (APS-U update, Aug 2025; APS News, Jun 2026). APS-U itself was formally completed (CD-4), announced in Feb 2026. The source is still the two planar 3.0 cm undulators (APS ID table, Sep 2026): neither the superconducting SCAPE undulators (designed for source-based polarization control over 2.7–27 keV; fully circular light only in the first harmonic) nor the permanent-magnet X-undulator alternative (1 m prototype design, from 2.6 keV) is installed, so circular and vertical-linear polarization still come from the crystal phase retarders, which cover about 2.7–14 keV.

tagline: Twisting X-rays into left- and right-handed corkscrews to reveal hidden magnetism in matter squeezed to millions of atmospheres.
summary: POLAR is a 78-metre beamline at Sector 4 of Argonne's Advanced Photon Source (APS) that uses polarized X-rays to study magnetism one element at a time. Its undulators make X-rays whose electric field swings side to side; thin diamond crystals turn this into left- or right-handed circular polarization, a corkscrew, and flip the handedness many times a second. At an element's absorption edge, the X-ray energy at which its inner electrons absorb strongly, a magnetic material absorbs the two handednesses differently, by a fraction of a percent to a few percent; the difference reveals how strongly that element is magnetized and in which direction. The upgraded source lets POLAR focus this light to 100–400 nm, small enough for samples squeezed between two diamond tips to 3 megabars (about 3 million atmospheres), chilled to 1.4 degrees above absolute zero in a 9-tesla magnet. First users came in 2025.

whatAPSUEnables.text: The upgraded ring's electron beam is about 19 times narrower horizontally (14.5 µm root-mean-square width in the 2021 flat-beam design instead of 275 µm) and spreads less, so POLAR's mirrors can focus polarized X-rays to 100–400 nm; before the upgrade the polarized beam at Sector 4 was about 15 µm across. Smaller beams allow smaller samples, and so higher pressures: the design goal is about 6 megabars, against about 0.5 megabar for magnetic measurements before the upgrade and 3.6 megabars at Earth's centre. The coherent fraction, the share of the beam whose waves march in step as lens-free imaging requires, is about 200 times larger at 10 keV, for magnetic images aimed at 10–50 nm. In a 300 nm spot the planned gain is about 100 times more polarized flux. The caveats: in 2026 the beamline lists 3 megabars and 400 nm for magnetic imaging, and the polarizing undulators that would avoid the phase plates' 5–30-fold flux loss and reach above 14 keV are not yet installed.
quantitative: Horizontal electron beam size 275 µm → 14.5 µm and divergence 11 → 2.9 µrad, APS vs APS-U brightness mode (POLAR town hall 2021)
Coherent fraction at 10 keV increased ×200 vs the pre-upgrade APS (POLAR workshop slides 2023; POLAR town hall 2021)
Focused polarized beam: ~15×15 µm² (pre-upgrade 4-ID-D, toroid + KB) → 100–200 nm (4-ID-G KB) and 300–400 nm (4-ID-H KB) (APS 4-ID-D page 2018; APS beamline directory 2026)

techniques.name: X-ray magnetic circular dichroism
techniques.text: X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) compares how strongly a material absorbs left- and right-circularly polarized X-rays at one element's absorption edge. A difference appears only where that element's magnetic moments are, on average, aligned; its size and sign reveal their net strength and direction along the beam. With hard X-rays the effect is small, typically 0.1–6% of the absorption step, so the design calls for flipping the handedness about 13–15 times a second and using lock-in detection, which keeps only the signal that flips in step, aiming to detect differences of ten parts per million. At the L edges of 4d and 5d metals, 'sum rules' split the signal into spin and orbital magnetism; at the K edges of 3d metals and the L edges of rare earths it comes from magnetism induced in outer electrons and is read more qualitatively. Edges above the phase plates' limit of about 14 keV, such as actinide L edges, await a future polarizing undulator.

techniques.name: X-ray (magnetic) linear dichroism
techniques.text: X-ray linear dichroism (XLD) compares absorption of horizontally and vertically polarized X-rays. It reveals lopsided electron clouds (orbitals), ferroelectric distortions and the axis along which magnetic moments line up; the magnetic part, X-ray magnetic linear dichroism (XMLD), works even in antiferromagnets, whose neighbouring moments point in opposite directions and cancel, so they show no circular dichroism. POLAR makes vertical polarization by setting the phase retarders as a half-wave plate, about 80% vertically polarized at low energies and 95% at high energies. At 4-ID-H a field of up to 1 tesla across the beam is available for XMLD.

techniques.name: Polarized X-ray absorption near-edge / fine structure
techniques.text: X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy scans the X-ray energy across an element's absorption edge. The edge's position and shape reveal the element's charge state (valence) and its surroundings, for example when pressure pushes an electron out of a rare earth's localized 4f shell into the shared sea of conduction electrons. POLAR uses it to follow valence changes, mixed valence and the Kondo effect, in which conduction electrons screen a local magnetic moment, in materials containing ytterbium, europium, cerium or uranium, and orbital occupancy in 5d oxides under pressure. Spectra are taken in transmission through the diamond anvils or by fluorescence, usually together with magnetic circular dichroism on the same sample.

techniques.name: X-ray resonant magnetic scattering / diffraction
techniques.text: In X-ray resonant magnetic scattering (XRMS) the energy is tuned to an element's absorption edge and the beam is diffracted by a crystal. Magnetic order with its own repeat pattern, such as an antiferromagnet whose moments alternate, adds weak diffraction spots where the atomic lattice alone gives none; the resonance boosts them and makes them element-specific. POLAR does this on the 4-ID-G Huber diffractometer, whose detector arm is split 25° between an area detector and a polarization analyzer that separates scattered light polarized perpendicular (σ) and parallel (π) to the scattering plane. Samples can be cooled to 4 K, placed in a ±2 T magnet, squeezed in mini diamond cells to 20 GPa, or strained.

techniques.name: X-ray resonant magnetic reflectivity
techniques.text: X-ray resonant magnetic reflectivity (XRMR) reflects polarized X-rays off a stack of thin films at shallow angles. Waves reflected at each interface interfere, so the reflected intensity versus angle encodes how magnetism changes with depth, layer by layer, and can pick up magnetism at an interface only an atomic layer or so thick. POLAR measures the mirror-like (specular) reflection and the diffuse scattering around it with circular dichroism. A fully in-vacuum setup reaches down to 2.75–3.4 keV, the L edges of ruthenium, rhodium and palladium, in fields up to 2 tesla.

techniques.name: Dichroic ptychography and tomography
techniques.text: Coherent diffractive imaging makes a picture without an image-forming lens. In ptychography a coherent, focused beam steps across the sample in overlapping spots, a camera records the speckle pattern at each, and a computer finds the one image that explains them all; with circularly polarized light tuned to a magnetic edge, that image shows magnetic domains. Rotating the sample and repeating builds a 3D map of the magnetization direction (vector tomography). POLAR's setup combines 100–200 nm coherent beams, a precision air-bearing stage and detectors planned at 2.7, 4 and 10 m. The goal is 10–50 nm; the 2026 beamline directory quotes 400 nm for dichroic imaging, and POLAR's 3D reconstruction pipeline has so far been demonstrated on data taken at MAX IV in Sweden, not at POLAR.

techniques.name: Spectroscopy in the diamond anvil cell at extreme pressure, low temperature and high field
techniques.text: The extreme-conditions instrument combines a diamond anvil cell with low temperature and high field. The sample, smaller than a grain of salt, sits between the flat tips (culets) of two diamonds in a non-magnetic copper–beryllium cell, and helium-filled membranes raise or lower the pressure remotely while it is cold. Diamond is fairly transparent to hard X-rays, but it absorbs noticeably at the 5–9 keV edges of transition metals and rare earths: at the iron edge 1 mm passes only about 10%. POLAR therefore uses perforated or partially perforated anvils that leave just 0.1–0.2 mm in the beam. Pressure is read from the fluorescence of a ruby chip below 100 GPa (1 megabar), from the diamond's Raman signal above it, or from X-ray diffraction of a gold, silver or platinum marker. Double-stage or toroidal anvils are planned for multi-megabar work.

scienceCases.title: Magnetism and valence of rare earths and actinides at multi-megabar pressure
scienceCases.text: Squeezing a metal pushes its atoms together until its electrons rearrange: a magnetic atom can lose its magnetism, or the material can become a superconductor. In rare-earth and actinide materials, pressure tips the balance between two rival effects: magnetic coupling between atoms through the conduction electrons (the RKKY interaction) and the screening of each atom's moment by those electrons (the Kondo effect). Examples include ytterbium's crossover between a magnetic 4f¹³ and a non-magnetic 4f¹⁴ state, superconductivity near mixed valence, plutonium, and the unexplained 'hidden order' of URu₂Si₂. POLAR follows them with absorption spectroscopy and magnetic circular dichroism at rare-earth and 5d L edges at 4-ID-H, at 1.4–300 K, up to 9 T and toward the 6-megabar goal. Actinide M edges at 3.3–4 keV lie within today's polarization range; their L edges at about 16–22 keV need the future polarizing undulator.

scienceCases.title: Hydrides and the hunt for room-temperature superconductivity
scienceCases.text: Hydrogen-rich compounds such as lanthanum hydride (LaH₁₀) superconduct at up to about 250 K (−23 °C), close to room temperature, but only at around 1.7–1.9 megabars. Samples at such pressures are only micrometres across, so they need beams smaller still. POLAR's 0.1–0.4 µm polarized beams and megabar diamond-cell instruments are aimed at the electronic and magnetic structure of these hydrides and related sulfides, and at iron hydrides, where magnetism and superconductivity interplay. The question is whether magnetism plays a role in these materials.

scienceCases.title: Quantum materials under pressure: spin liquids, Mott and Kondo physics
scienceCases.text: Pressure is a clean tuning knob: it changes how electrons hop and interact between atoms without adding impurities. It can turn an insulator into a metal, or freeze or melt exotic magnetic states. POLAR targets 4d and 5d oxides such as honeycomb 'Kitaev' candidates for a quantum spin liquid, in which the moments never settle into order, and Sr₂IrO₄-type iridates; iridium-edge magnetic circular dichroism in a diamond cell was already done at 8 GPa and 11 K at POLAR's predecessor, 4-ID-D. Other targets are insulator–metal transitions in stiff transition-metal oxides, which need very high pressure, and spin freezing in 'frustrated' magnets, whose moments cannot all satisfy their neighbours at once. The weak, diffuse scattering from short-range magnetic order needs the brightest possible beam.

scienceCases.title: Imaging magnetic, chiral and polar (ferroelectric) textures
scienceCases.text: Magnets and ferroelectrics break up into regions of uniform orientation (domains), swirls and knots such as skyrmions that could one day store data. Coherent polarized X-rays can image these textures inside a crystal, not only at its surface. POLAR's dichroic ptychography and tomography target magnetic and antiferromagnetic domains (the latter through linear-dichroism contrast), skyrmion strings and polar vortices, aiming at 10–50 nm by lens-free reconstruction or about 100 nm by direct scanning. The examples the team cites were not measured at POLAR: ferroelectric 'incommensurate spin crystals' in SrRuO₃/PbTiO₃ trilayers at the pre-upgrade 4-ID-D, and the 3D magnetization of Nd₂Fe₁₄B magnet pillars from MAX IV data, reconstructed with the pipeline now implemented at POLAR.

scienceCases.title: Strain gradients and flexomagnetism in thin membranes (first POLAR users)
scienceCases.text: Bending a thin crystal stretches one side and compresses the other, and that strain gradient can create magnetism, an effect called flexomagnetism. POLAR's first users, a University of Wisconsin team in the January–May 2025 run, studied it in thin materials for future microelectronics. A related University of Wisconsin–Madison group writes strain gradients of about 10⁶ m⁻¹ into GdAuGe films by helium-ion implantation and lists nanoprobe X-ray magnetic circular dichroism among the measurements needed; gadolinium's L₃ edge at 7.243 keV lies within POLAR's phase-plate range. That the first users came from this group is our inference, and the group's own published nanodiffraction was done at another synchrotron, the National Synchrotron Light Source II, not at POLAR.

scienceCases.title: Interfaces and heterostructures at low photon energy
scienceCases.text: Where two thin layers meet, magnetism can appear that neither has on its own, for example a moment induced in a normally non-magnetic metal by a magnetic neighbour. POLAR measures such interfaces element by element. On the 4-ID-G diffractometer an in-vacuum setup reaches the L edges of ruthenium, rhodium and palladium at 2.75–3.4 keV, as well as the K edges of 3d metals, for magnetic circular and linear dichroism and resonant reflectivity in fields up to ±2 T. Targets include proximity-induced moments and 4d and 5d layers with strong spin–orbit coupling, the link between an electron's spin and its orbital motion; uniaxial strain cells and voltage-bias cells are also supported.

scienceCases.title: Magnetic X-ray emission spectroscopy at extreme conditions (MagXES, in development)
scienceCases.text: X-ray emission spectroscopy analyses the X-rays a sample re-emits after absorbing the beam; their spectrum carries a signature of local magnetism, even in materials whose atomic moments point every which way and add up to nothing. A 2024 US Department of Energy Early Career award to G. Fabbris ($550,000 a year for five years) funds a magnetic X-ray emission spectroscopy (MagXES) instrument at POLAR, built around new spectrometer designs, for low temperature, high pressure and high field. Its status in 2026 has not been confirmed.

insertionDevices.name: APS30#4 (upstream)
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet undulator (out-of-vacuum, variable gap)
insertionDevices.notes: 79 periods (77 effective; 79 × 30 mm = 2.37 m magnetic length, computed). Device minimum gap 9.0 mm, admin minimum 9.17 mm, user minimum 9.4 mm. Keff 2.62 → E1 2.56 keV. 214 kW/mrad², 10.2 kW at 200 mA. Not a 'short' device. A reused (refurbished) pre-upgrade magnetic structure: the IPAC'24 undulator table lists the 3.0-cm period only as 'Existing IDs' (3 full-length plus 5 canted), while the new APS-U periods are 1.35, 1.4, 2.1, 2.5 and 2.8 cm; full-length devices are ~2.4 m (Dejus et al. 2024, Table 1). FDR: 'Linear 30 mm, 2 × 2.3 m at SSC' (APS-U FDR 2019).

insertionDevices.name: APS30#9 (downstream)
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet undulator (out-of-vacuum, variable gap)
insertionDevices.notes: 79 periods; device minimum gap 9.0 mm, admin minimum 9.06 mm, user minimum 9.1 mm. Keff 2.64 → E1 2.54 keV. 215 kW/mrad², 10.4 kW at 200 mA.

insertionDevices.name: In-line phase shifter (S04ID:ILPS) with corrector
insertionDevices.notes: Sets the electron path delay so that radiation from both undulators adds in phase. APS-U installed 11 phase shifters with correctors in in-line sectors (Dejus et al. 2024). Exposed in POLAR's Bluesky configuration (POLAR Bluesky config). The phase-shifter length is unpublished; the zero in the source table is a placeholder.

insertionDevices.name: SCAPE (Superconducting Arbitrarily Polarizing Emitter), 2 units, NOT INSTALLED
insertionDevices.notes: Planned 'mature scope' replacement for the two planar devices. Pure circular polarization comes only in the first harmonic; higher harmonics give linear (H or V) or elliptical light with Pc tunable to ~75–90% (PDR), which is how 14–27 keV would be covered (APS-U PDR 2017). FDR: 35 mm × 1.3 m (conservative), possibly 30 mm and up to 1.8 m. PDR: 3.0 cm × 1.5 m in a single ~4.5 m cryostat. Fast switching would use ~30 µrad alternating orbit bumps at up to 10 Hz, or ~6 A undulator current bumps (APS-U FDR 2019; APS-U PDR 2017). A 0.5 m prototype (30 mm period, 16.5 periods, 10 mm magnetic gap, NbTi, 540 A operating current) was tested in 2021 (Kasa et al. 2021). The 2021 town hall planned replacement for ~2026 (POLAR town hall 2021). It requires a ~6 mm-ID round vacuum chamber. Installation is not confirmed as of Sept 2026 (APS ID table, Sep 2026).

insertionDevices.name: X-undulator (alternative future polarizing source), PROTOTYPE STAGE
insertionDevices.type: fixed-gap APPLE-X-like pure permanent-magnet undulator with force-compensation arrays
insertionDevices.polarization: all states (circular, elliptical, linear at any angle)
insertionDevices.notes: Four NdFeB Halbach arrays around an 8.5 mm bore (6.0/7.5 mm ID/OD round chamber); max Keff 2.6 → 2.6 keV minimum. K and polarization are set by longitudinal array motion. Switching takes 1 Hz via quarter-period shift, or ~5 Hz with a dual-XU detuning scheme. 1-m prototype design (Qian et al. 2024, IPAC'24). Funded by a 2023 LDRD 'Force-neutral fast polarization switching X-undulator for the POLAR beamline' (Haskel CV 2024). Not installed.

source.canting: None. The two planar undulators are in line (collinear) in the 4-ID straight, separated by a phase shifter (APS-U FDR 2019, ch. 3; APS ID table, Sep 2026). Before the upgrade, sector 4 was canted, with a circularly polarizing electromagnetic undulator (CPU, 12.8 cm period) feeding soft-x-ray 4-ID-C and, in 2002, Undulator A (3.3 cm) feeding hard-x-ray 4-ID-D (Srajer 2002); by 2018 the 4-ID-D source was a 2.4 m, 3.5 cm-period SmCo undulator (APS 4-ID-D page 2018). APS-U gave the whole straight to POLAR's hard-x-ray line (APS News 2020).
source.frontEnd: Standard APS-U High-Heat-Load front end, windowless with differential pumping, rated 21 kW total and 590 kW/mrad² peak (APS-U FDR 2019, ch. 3; APS-U FDR 2019). The design is based on the 28-ID HHLFE. Elements in order: LPPS, storage-ring valve, burn-through fixed mask BTFM1, fixed mask FM2, collimator, GRID XBPM, FM3, photon shutter PS2 with intensity monitor, redundant safety shutters SS1/SS2, wall collimator, front-end valve, exit mask with XBPM2, exit collimator, beamline isolation valve (APS-U FDR 2019, ch. 3). Exit mask aperture is 2 × 2 mm (H × V) at ~25.4 m and the exit collimator is 5 × 5 mm at ~26.1 m (APS-U FDR 2019). Total power when the undulator is tuned to 2.8 keV (linear) is ~16 kW, with ~512 W/mm² on the white-beam slits at 27 m (APS-U FDR 2019).
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence: Electron beam at the ID source point, from the FDR Table 1.1 design (APS-U FDR 2019, Table 1.1). Brightness mode (324 bunches, 42 pm): σx = 14.7 µm, σx' = 2.8 µrad, σy = 3.2 µm, σy' = 1.3 µrad. Timing mode (48 bunches, 32 pm effective): σx = 12.9 µm, σx' = 2.5 µrad, σy = 8.8 µm, σy' = 3.7 µrad. The 2021 town hall quotes σx = 14.5 µm and σx' = 2.9 µrad, vs 275 µm and 11 µrad for the old APS (POLAR town hall 2021). The single-electron photon terms at 10 keV for L ≈ 2.4 m are σr ≈ √(2λL)/4π ≈ 2 µm and σr' ≈ √(λ/2L) ≈ 5 µrad (computed here, approximate). The two undulators sit about ±1.3 m from the straight-section center, so focusing optics see two longitudinally separated sources. PDR ray tracing for ±1 m sources showed slightly asymmetric KB spots, mitigated with defining slits (APS-U PDR 2017).

components.name: Upstream undulator APS30#4
components.distanceNote: Approximate: the centre of the upstream device, inferred because no coordinate is published. Two ~2.4 m devices and a phase shifter share the ~5 m straight section.
components.text: The first of two 2.4-metre undulators: rows of alternating magnets that steer the 6 GeV electrons through 79 gentle wiggles, each adding to a bright, narrow X-ray beam. The light leaves with its electric field oscillating side to side (horizontal linear polarization), the raw material POLAR later twists into circular polarization. With a 3.0 cm magnet period its lowest (first-harmonic) energy sits near 2.6 keV at the smallest gap, and higher odd harmonics, at odd multiples of that energy, reach 27 keV. Its magnet structure is reused from the original APS.

components.name: In-line phase shifter + corrector
components.distanceNote: Approximate and inferred: between the two undulators, near the centre of the straight section.
components.text: A short, adjustable magnet between the two undulators that delays the electrons by a tiny, precise amount, so they enter the second undulator in step with the light from the first. The two undulators' light then adds up instead of partly cancelling. Its setting follows the undulator gap, and corrector magnets keep the orbit straight; the upgrade installed 11 such units in sectors with two undulators in line.

specs.purpose: constructive interference of the two undulators

components.name: Downstream undulator APS30#9
components.distanceNote: Approximate and inferred: the centre of the downstream device.
components.text: The second undulator, of the same design and in line with the first; together they roughly double the flux. Both make only horizontally polarized light. Superconducting Arbitrarily Polarizing Emitter (SCAPE) undulators or a permanent-magnet 'X-undulator' could one day make circularly polarized light directly and replace this pair, but neither is installed as of September 2026.

components.name: High-heat-load front end (windowless)
components.distanceNote: Schematic: shown as one unit centred at 20 m. The front end runs from ~13 m to inside the FOE (~26 m), through the ratchet (shield) wall at ~23.6–24.4 m (2021 plan and elevation). Individual element positions are not published; the model follows the 2021 elevation drawing for the last few metres (photon shutter ~22.2 m, tandem safety shutters ~22.7–23.4 m, wall collimator in the ratchet wall) and the FDR element order upstream.
components.text: The safety gateway between the accelerator and the beamline, mostly inside the concrete shield tunnel. Water-cooled masks absorb the outer parts of the beam, monitors check its pointing, and heavy shutters stop it whenever people need to enter the first hutch. It is rated for 21 kW of X-ray power, about a dozen hair dryers' worth. It has no beryllium window: differential pumping separates its vacuum from the beamline's, which preserves low-energy flux and coherence.

components.name: Front-end exit mask (with XBPM2)
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.16.
components.text: A water-cooled copper block with a 2 × 2 mm hole that passes only the bright central part of the beam and turns the rest into heat. A beam-position monitor built into it checks that the beam stays centred. It sits on the last front-end table, already inside the first hutch.

components.name: Front-end exit collimator
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.16.
components.text: A heavy tungsten block with a 5 × 5 mm hole. It blocks bremsstrahlung, very high-energy gamma rays made when electrons hit stray gas molecules in the ring, everywhere except a narrow pencil around the beam, which a stop further down then catches. The upgrade narrowed this hole to help beamlines whose monochromators shift the beam only slightly.

components.name: High-heat-load white-beam slits (4ID-SL-1)
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.16; the 2021 plan shows the slit at ~26.8–27.6 m (scaled).
components.text: Four tungsten-edged jaws trim the raw 'white' beam, still containing all energies, to its bright central cone and so protect the optics downstream. With the undulators tuned to 2.8 keV the beam here carries about 512 watts per square millimetre, roughly eight times the power density at the surface of the Sun. Even opened to the full 2.8 keV cone (0.92 × 0.92 mm) they pass only 432 W of the roughly 16 kW total; the typical opening is 0.5 × 0.5 mm.

specs.maxPowerThroughSlit: 432 W (0.92 × 0.92 mm² at 27 m, undulators tuned to 2.8 keV; FDR Table 4.15)

components.name: White-beam mirrors M1 + M2 (flat + bendable)
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.16 (both mirrors share one vessel). The 2021 plan shows the tank at ~27.6–29.2 m (scaled).
components.text: Two super-polished silicon mirrors, each met at a grazing angle of just 3 milliradians (0.17°), bounce the beam sideways and back, leaving it parallel and about 4 mm to one side. Each carries stripes of bare silicon, rhodium and platinum; a mirror reflects only below a cut-off energy that depends on its coating, so the chosen stripe removes unwanted higher harmonics, X-rays at multiples of the chosen energy. The first, flat mirror absorbs much of the heat (254 W at 2.8 keV); the second can be bent to cancel the heat bumps on the first mirror and the monochromator crystal.

components.name: Photon mask / pink-beam stop (4ID-PM-1)
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.16.
components.text: A cooled block that catches whatever part of the raw beam the mirrors did not reflect. Only the mirror-filtered beam, called 'pink' because part of the spectrum has been removed, continues to the monochromator.

components.name: Beam-viewing flags + cameras (4-ID-A)
components.distanceNote: Approximate; shown at the post-mirror flag. The Bluesky configuration defines two 4-ID-A flag cameras, PostMirrBeam (between the mirror tank, ending ~29.2 m, and the DCM vessel, starting ~30.15 m on the 2021 plan, so ~29.7 m) and PostMonoBeam (after the DCM, ~31.3 m). Positions are not published.
components.text: Fluorescent screens that swing into the beam and glow where the X-rays hit, watched by cameras, so staff can see where the beam is after the mirrors and after the monochromator. They are used for alignment and to check a change of mirror stripe or crystal.

components.name: Double-crystal monochromator (vertical, Si / SiC)
components.distanceNote: Centre of the DCM vessel on the 2021 'Sector 4 2024' plan and elevation (~30.15–31.05 m, scaled; drawn as a drum ~0.9 m across in the elevation). FDR Table 4.16 listed 30.0 m when the DCM was still specified as horizontal-deflecting; as built it is vertical-deflecting.
components.text: The monochromator picks a single X-ray energy: two perfect crystals reflect only the wavelength that fits their atomic spacing at the set angle (Bragg's law), selecting the energy to about one part in 7,000. Turning them scans the energy across an element's absorption edge, where the magnetic signal lives, and liquid-nitrogen cooling keeps them flat under the heat load. They deflect the beam vertically, so the horizontally polarized light stays perpendicular to the plane of reflection (σ geometry) at every angle. A second pair of silicon carbide crystals, for energies near 2.8 keV, would matter only once polarization is made in the source; whether it is installed and in use is not published.

specs.geometry: vertical deflection: linear-H light reflects in σ geometry
specs.SiC crystals: for source-made polarization near 2.8 keV, where Si(111) reflects at a Bragg angle ≈ 45° and would suppress π (vertical) polarization; 6H-SiC(0006) reflects at 61.4°

components.name: Monochromatic-beam slits (4ID-SL-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16 gives 31.1 m; the 2021 plan shows a small device at ~31.2 m, just downstream of the as-built DCM tank (used here).
components.text: In-vacuum jaws just after the monochromator that trim the edges of the now single-energy beam. Cleaning it up here stops stray and scattered light from travelling on to the polarizing optics.

components.name: Collimators and white-beam stop
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16: secondary collimator 31.3 m, photon mask/WB stop 31.7 m, primary bremsstrahlung collimator 32.0 m. Behind the as-built DCM the 2021 plan shows these small items ~0.25 m further downstream (~31.55, 32.0 and 32.3 m); the model uses the plan values, centred on the WB stop.
components.text: Shielding that makes sure only the monochromatic beam, offset 15.6 mm by the crystals, leaves the first hutch. A tungsten stop intercepts the beam that went straight through the crystals, and collimators block stray high-energy radiation (bremsstrahlung). The monochromator's vertical offset is what lets the stop catch the straight-through line while the useful beam passes clear of it.

components.name: Diamond phase retarders (quarter-wave plates)
components.distanceNote: Centre of the tank on the 2021 plan (~33.0–33.9 m, scaled; two plate stages drawn as circles). FDR Table 4.16: 33.2 m. This is the existing 4-ID-D tank, reused.
components.text: The heart of POLAR: thin diamond plates that make the beam's side-to-side polarization circular. Each plate, tilted one to two hundredths of a degree off the angle at which it would reflect the beam, splits the light into two polarization components that travel at slightly different speeds, the principle of a quarter-wave plate for visible light. With the plane of reflection at 45° to the polarization, a quarter-wave delay makes the light circular; the side of the tilt sets the handedness, and two plates in series give vertical linear polarization. A piezo actuator rocks the plate to flip the handedness, about 15 times a second in the design, with about 98% circular polarization. The price: the plates work only up to about 14 keV and lose a factor of 5–30 in flux.

specs.plates: pr1, pr2: C(111)/C(220) diamond; pr3: Si(111)
specs.principle: Bragg-transmission quarter-wave plate (Hirano et al. 1993); diamond plates after Lang & Srajer (1995)
specs.Quarter-wave offset: ~42″ at 10 keV, ~80″ at 8 keV off Bragg (500 µm C(111), calculated)
specs.fluxCost: ×5–30 flux loss; 5–30% intensity asymmetry between helicities

components.name: Monochromatic station shutter (4ID-SH-1)
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.16; the 2021 plan shows it at ~34.2–35.5 m.
components.text: A heavy safety shutter, the gate between the optics hutch and the experiments. Controlled by the personnel safety system, it lets beam into 4-ID-B only when the hutches downstream have been searched and locked.

components.name: Shielded beam transport (4-ID-A → 4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Spans ~36.1–50.5 m on the 2021 plan (scaled); midpoint given. Pipe stands at ~37.8, 39.0, 41.2, 43.3, 45.3, 46.5 and 48.8 m.
components.text: A 14-metre vacuum pipe wrapped in lead shielding carries the beam across the experiment-hall floor, so people can walk safely beside it while the beam is on. It rests on stands every few metres and passes a small legacy mini-hutch before entering 4-ID-B.

components.name: 4-ID-B entrance slits (bslt)
components.distanceNote: Approximate. The FDR places a mono slit (SL-3) just upstream of the toroids (47.3 m in the FDR layout); the as-built toroids are at 53.7 m. Position inferred.
components.text: Adjustable jaws at the entrance of 4-ID-B that set how much of the beam reaches the focusing optics, and so the balance between spot size and brightness. Their exact position is inferred from the design order.

components.name: Toroidal focusing mirror M3 (bendable)
components.distanceNote: From the 2021 town-hall slide 'Reflectivities/cut-offs', which places the toroidal double mirrors at 53.7 and 54.5 m.
components.text: A curved, metal-coated mirror that gently focuses the whole beam to a spot a few tens of micrometres wide (about 30 × 5 µm), for experiments that need many photons rather than a tiny spot. Bending it moves the focus to the 4-ID-G diffractometer at 67.2 m or the 4-ID-H magnet at 73.3 m. Like the first mirrors it also removes unwanted harmonics, and it slides out of the way when the finer focusing optics are used.

specs.stripes: Pd sagittal cylinder; Si and Pt flats (SRI 2021)

components.name: Cylinder/flat mirror M4
components.distanceNote: From the same 2021 town-hall slide (mirrors at 53.7 and 54.5 m).
components.text: A second mirror that sends the beam back parallel to its original path, a few millimetres to the side, and completes the focusing. Its palladium, silicon and platinum stripes, together with those of the first mirror pair, suppress unwanted harmonics across the whole 2.7–27 keV range.

specs.stripes: Pd flat; Si and Pt sagittal cylinders (SRI 2021)

components.name: Post-toroid beam-viewing flag (4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: just downstream of the M4 vessel (54.5 m); inferred from the device name only.
components.text: A fluorescent screen and camera just after the focusing mirrors, used to see the beam while the mirror pair is aligned. Its position is inferred from the device name.

components.name: Diamond vacuum window
components.distanceNote: Approximate. A small component on the 2021 plan ~0.8 m after M4 (the FDR window was 0.8 m after M4). The FDR specified 'Be or diamond'; Bluesky confirms a diamond window with x/y stages in 4-ID-B.
components.text: A thin diamond sheet that separates the windowless, ultra-high vacuum of the optics from the experiment section while letting X-rays pass almost untouched. Diamond, chosen over the more common beryllium, barely disturbs the beam's coherence, the in-step quality that coherent imaging relies on. The window sits on motorized stages.

components.name: In-line X-ray polarimeter
components.distanceNote: Approximate. Placed on the 4-ID-B optics table (~57.5–60 m on the 2021 plan) following the FDR component order; the FDR position (53.4 m) predates the toroid move.
components.text: A polarization meter that checks the phase retarders' work. A retractable foil scatters a little of the beam through 90° into two detectors set at right angles; X-rays scatter least along the direction in which their electric field oscillates, so the two signals show how much of the light is linearly polarized, and along which axis. Rotating the assembly about the beam completes the measurement; the circular part follows from it for a fully polarized beam, or can be measured by inserting a phase plate as an analyzer.

components.name: Diamond XBPM / TetrAMM (4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: FDR component order, scaled to the 2021 plan.
components.text: A thin, nearly transparent diamond sensor that reports where the beam is. Its signal drives a feedback loop that nudges the monochromator's second crystal with piezo actuators, aiming to hold the beam direction steady to 0.1 µrad. Stations B, G and H each have their own feedback loop.

components.name: In-vacuum optical chopper
components.distanceNote: Approximate: FDR component order, scaled to the 2021 plan.
components.text: A spinning slotted wheel that blinks the beam on and off up to 4,000 times a second. Comparing 'on' with 'off' lets the electronics subtract their own background signal (dark current), essential when the design aims to detect magnetic signals as small as ten parts per million. It works alongside the slower helicity flip: one lock-in measurement follows the chopper, another the dichroism.

specs.use: double lock-in: dark current at the chopper frequency, dichroism at the helicity frequency

components.name: Attenuators / filters (4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: FDR component order, scaled to the 2021 plan.
components.text: Thin metal foils that slide into the beam to dim it in steps, for alignment and to protect detectors and delicate samples from too much light. They sit in a standard APS filter box.

components.name: Bendable KB mirrors 'KB3' (2 T station)
components.distanceNote: Approximate. Inferred from the 2021 plan table position upstream of the electromagnet; FDR: 55.1 m relative to the magnet at 55.8 m.
components.text: A pair of Kirkpatrick–Baez (KB) mirrors, one focusing vertically and the other horizontally, whose curvature can be adjusted to tune the spot size. They focus the beam onto samples in the 2-tesla electromagnet. The 2017 design called for spots down to about 10 µm; the as-built value is not published.

specs.focus: down to ~10 µm (PDR 2017 design value; as-built value not published)

components.name: Incident-intensity monitor I0 (4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: FDR component order, scaled to the 2021 plan.
components.text: An intensity monitor that counts the X-rays heading into the sample, so absorption can be measured as a ratio that ignores small flickers in the beam. It is an ion chamber or photodiode read by a current amplifier.

components.name: 2 T electromagnet station (existing)
components.distanceNote: Approximate, measured from the 2021 'Sector 4 2024' plan (scale ±0.3 m). FDR: 55.8 m in its earlier layout.
components.text: A water-cooled electromagnet inherited from POLAR's predecessor, 4-ID-D, whose field can be ramped and reversed quickly, without liquid helium in the magnet. It serves films, crystals and lightly compressed samples: up to 2 T at small pole gaps, about 0.8 T with a diamond anvil cell in place, and above 10 K with a flow cryostat. It is configured in the control software but not listed as an end station in the 2026 beamline directory, so whether it is offered to users is unconfirmed.

specs.field: up to 2 T (≈0.8 T with DAC gap)

components.name: Transmission photodiode I (4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: a feature on the 2021 plan just downstream of the magnet.
components.text: A photodiode behind the magnet that measures how many X-rays made it through the sample. The dip in transmission at an element's absorption edge, and its small change with the light's handedness, is the signal.

components.name: Diamond XBPM, filters, slits (4-ID-G entrance)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: the start of the 4-ID-G optics table, ~64.1 m on the 2021 plan.
components.text: The gatekeepers of 4-ID-G: a diamond beam-position monitor, a filter box and adjustable jaws that steady, dim and shape the beam before it is focused. The monitor feeds this station's own feedback loop to the monochromator.

components.name: Transfocator (Be compound refractive lenses)
components.distanceNote: 2 m upstream of the diffractometer (2021 town hall). The 2021 plan shows the CRL at ~65.25 m.
components.text: A stack of tiny curved beryllium lenses that focus X-rays by refraction. X-rays bend only very slightly in any material, so many lenses are needed in a row; like adding reading glasses, sliding more of its eight lens groups into the beam strengthens the focus. Because the focal length changes with energy, software picks the combination for each energy and spot size. It gives a spot about 2 × 0.9 µm, between the mirrors' broad focus and the nano-focus, over 3–20 keV.

components.name: KB1 nano-focusing mirrors (100 mm from focus)
components.distanceNote: Approximate. Computed from the sample at 67.2 m minus the 100 mm working distance and half-lengths of the FDR KB1 mirrors (VFM 275 mm upstream of HFM 115 mm).
components.text: Two small, precisely curved Kirkpatrick–Baez mirrors, one focusing vertically and one horizontally, squeeze the beam to about 100 nanometres, roughly a thousand times thinner than a hair, just 10 centimetres in front of the sample. Their elliptical shape is accurate to within 0.5 nm (root-mean-square). The design gives 114 × 92 nm with 1.3 × 10¹³ photons per second at 10 keV; closing a slit for coherent imaging leaves 1.6 × 10¹² photons per second in 200 × 200 nm.

components.name: Huber diffractometer (horizontal scattering)
components.distanceNote: Sample position: toroid focus point 67.2 m (2021 town hall) matches the 2021 plan (~67.3 m). FDR 2019 had the diffractometer at 61.3 m in a different hutch arrangement.
components.text: A precision 'robot arm and turntable' that holds the sample and swings detectors around it, to find the exact angles at which X-rays reflect from the repeating rows of atoms in a crystal, and from the repeating pattern of their magnetic moments. It scatters in the horizontal plane and omits the usual vertical circle, leaving room for bulky magnets and cryostats. Its detector arm splits into two branches 25° apart, one with an area detector and one with a polarization analyzer.

specs.geometry: 4S+2D horizontal (τ, μ, χ, φ, γ, δ)

components.name: ±2 T HTS split-pair magnet (diffractometer)
components.distanceNote: Mounted on the diffractometer at the sample position.
components.text: A compact superconducting magnet, cooled by a closed-cycle refrigerator rather than liquid helium, that wraps a field of up to 2 tesla, about 40,000 times Earth's, around the sample. It can point along the beam for spectroscopy or across it for diffraction, ramping from zero to 2 T in five minutes. Its high-temperature-superconductor coils leave a 60.4 mm gap for cryostats, mini diamond cells and strain cells.

components.name: Imaging stack (dichroic ptychography)
components.distanceNote: Operating position: it replaces the open Eulerian cradle on the diffractometer base at the 67.2 m sample point. The 3D model shows it parked on a cart beside the diffractometer so both configurations can be seen.
components.text: An ultra-steady sample stage for coherent imaging that swaps in for the diffractometer's cradle. From the bottom up it stacks tilts, translations, a 360° air-bearing rotation and a nanometre-precision positioner, while interferometers register the sample against the beam. With it a computer can build 2D and 3D magnetic images from forward-scattered light (ptychography and tomography) or from crystal reflections (Bragg coherent diffraction imaging). The model shows it parked beside the diffractometer so both setups can be seen.

components.name: Vortex ME-4 fluorescence detector (SDD)
components.distanceNote: At the sample. Shown looking in from the outboard side just upstream of 90° (snout ~0.17 m from the sample), through the HTS magnet's radial opening and clear of the detector arm; the exact mounting is not published.
components.text: An energy-resolving detector that measures the characteristic X-rays (fluorescence) each element emits after absorbing the beam, so one element's signal can be picked out from the rest of the sample. This four-element silicon drift detector serves fluorescence-detected magnetic dichroism and absorption spectroscopy, and helps suppress fluorescence background in resonant scattering.

components.name: Polarization analyzer + APD (detector arm)
components.distanceNote: On the point-detector branch of the split detector arm, ~0.9 m from the sample (not published). Shown with the arm at 2θ = 60° toward the outboard side (the plan draws the ~2 m arm sweep there), which puts it 67.65 m along the beam.
components.text: A second crystal, set to reflect through close to 90°, passes only one polarization of the scattered light to a fast avalanche photodiode. Ordinary scattering from electric charge keeps the polarization, while magnetic scattering can rotate it, so a signal in the rotated channel shows that a faint reflection really comes from magnetism. The analyzer crystal is chosen to suit each element's edge energy.

specs.analyzerCrystals: PG(001), Cu, Au, Al, Si, Ge, LiF, MgO, Mo, Pd, Pt …

components.name: Eiger2 X 1M pixel detector (also Lambda 750k)
components.distanceNote: Variable 0.5–2 m from the sample on the PAD branch of the arm. Shown at 1.5 m with that branch at 2θ = 35° (25° from the analyzer branch), i.e. 68.4 m along the beam. For forward ptychography, detector distances of 2.7, 4 and 10 m are planned; 10 m would reach into 4-ID-H, unconfirmed.
components.text: A fast photon-counting X-ray camera with about a million pixels that records diffraction spots and the speckle patterns from which images of magnetic domains are reconstructed. On the detector arm it sits 0.5–2 m from the sample; a Lambda 750k detector is also available.

components.name: G/H station shutter (inferred)
components.distanceNote: Inferred. The 2021 town-hall elevation drawing shows an unlabelled shutter-sized box on a stand at ~69.6–69.9 m, just upstream of the 4-ID-G/H wall (scaled). The FDR (Table 4.16) listed a second monochromatic shutter, 4ID-SH-2, at the end of its diffractometer hutch (64.6 m in the 2019 layout). Identity, position and as-built status are not published.
components.text: Probably a safety shutter at the end of 4-ID-G, inferred from the drawings but not confirmed. The beamline's design paper says 4-ID-H can be entered to load a pressure cell, cool the big magnet or do maintenance while 4-ID-G takes beam, which requires a shutter or stop at this boundary.

components.name: Diamond XBPM (Sydor) at 4-ID-H entrance
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16. The magnet position (73.3 m) is unchanged between FDR and as-built, so the upstream H positions are kept.
components.text: A diamond beam-position monitor at the entrance of 4-ID-H. It feeds this station's own feedback loop to the monochromator crystal, keeping the beam locked on the tiny sample inside the big magnet.

components.name: 4-ID-H slits
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.16 (4ID-SL-6, an existing slit).
components.text: Jaws that set how much of the focusing mirrors is lit, trading a little flux for a cleaner, rounder spot. Because the two undulators sit one behind the other, the mirrors see two sources at slightly different distances; limiting the illuminated area removes the asymmetry this causes in the spot.

components.name: 4-ID-H attenuators
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.16.
components.text: Metal foils that slide into the beam to dim it, protecting detectors and fragile samples during alignment. They are the 4-ID-H counterpart of the filters in 4-ID-B.

components.name: KB2 long-working-distance mirrors (600 mm)
components.distanceNote: Approximate. FDR KB2 at 72.46 m (VFM) and 72.78 m (HFM) for a 400 mm WD; the as-built WD is 600 mm, so the mirrors sit ~0.2 m further upstream (computed).
components.text: Kirkpatrick–Baez focusing mirrors that stand well back, 60 cm from their focus, because the giant magnet's body is in the way. A longer working distance gives less demagnification, yet they still squeeze the beam to 300–400 nm. The working distance was raised from 400 to 600 mm to fit the 9-1-1 T magnet; the design spot is 414 × 212 nm with 2.1 × 10¹³ photons per second at 10 keV.

components.name: Incident-intensity monitor I0 (4-ID-H)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16 (4ID-BD-4), between the KB2 mirrors (ending ~72.7 m) and the magnet's upstream window.
components.text: An intensity monitor that counts the X-rays going into the magnet, so the sample's absorption can be measured as a ratio. Further channels measure the beam downstream.

components.name: 9-1-1 T superconducting magnet (vector)
components.distanceNote: Toroid focus point 73.3 m (2021 town hall). FDR gives 73.3–73.4 m; the 2021 plan confirms.
components.text: A large superconducting magnet cooled by a liquid-helium bath, with a 75 mm shaft down its middle for a diamond anvil cell. Its split coils make up to 9 T along the beam and 1 T in either direction across it, hence '9-1-1', and a variable-temperature insert cools the sample from 300 K down to 1.4 K, colder than outer space. Liquid helium was chosen over a cryocooler on purpose, because a cryocooler's vibrations would blur a 300 nm beam. Side windows give the fluorescence detector and the Raman pressure gauge a view of the sample, interferometers track drift as the field ramps (0–9 T in about 9 minutes), and the whole magnet slides aside to let the beam reach the 4 T magnet behind it.

components.name: Diamond anvil cell (double gas membrane)
components.distanceNote: At the centre of the magnet.
components.text: Two gem-quality diamonds with tips smaller than a pinhead squeeze the sample to millions of atmospheres: 3 megabars is listed as available in 2026, and about 6 megabars is the design goal. Helium-filled membranes, one to compress and one to decompress, change the pressure remotely while the cell sits cold inside the magnet. The non-magnetic copper–beryllium cell rides on a nanopositioner that keeps the sample under the beam.

specs.pressureControl: in-situ He gas membranes driven by remote pressure controllers (Bluesky devices ge_apply/ge_release)
specs.mount: x/y/z nanopositioner at the probe tip
specs.cell: non-magnetic CuBe, compression + decompression He membranes

components.name: Raman / ruby spectrometer (pressure gauge)
components.distanceNote: Optical access through the magnet's re-entrant side bore on the outboard side (SRI 2021 drawing).
components.text: A laser and spectrometer that read the pressure through a side window of the magnet. Below 100 GPa (1 megabar) the gauge is the shift of the red glow of a tiny ruby chip; above it, the shift of the Raman signal of the squeezed diamond tip. The same system can be used for Raman studies of the sample.

specs.calibration: ruby (<100 GPa), diamond Raman edge (>100 GPa)

components.name: Laser interferometers (sample position)
components.distanceNote: Heads on the magnet support, looking into the side bores.
components.text: Laser interferometers act as rulers that notice if the magnet or sample drifts across the beam while the field ramps up or down. A slow correction loop then uses the nanopositioner to steer the sample back under the sub-micrometre beam.

components.name: 7-element fluorescence detector (SDD)
components.distanceNote: At the sample, through a Be-windowed re-entrant side bore of the magnet (inboard side in the model; Raman uses the outboard bore). The FDR lists 74.2 m for the detector stand.
components.text: A seven-element silicon drift detector at a beryllium-windowed side port of the magnet that collects the X-rays the sample re-emits (fluorescence). It serves measurements that cannot be made by looking straight through the sample.

components.name: Transmission detector I (4-ID-H)
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.16 (4ID-BD-5).
components.text: A detector behind the magnet that measures the X-rays that made it through the diamonds and the sample. The dip at an absorption edge, and its tiny change when the light's handedness flips, is the main signal of the high-pressure measurements.

components.name: 4 T cryogen-free magnet (existing)
components.distanceNote: Approximate, from the 2021 plan (~76.3 m); the FDR gives 75.9 m ('small-bore 4 T magnet, existing').
components.text: A smaller, cryogen-free 4-tesla magnet inherited from 4-ID-D, at the end of the line. To reach it, the big 9-1-1 T magnet slides aside ('beam-pass' mode). It works with the broader beam from the toroidal mirrors, tens of micrometres across, because the nano-focusing mirrors focus at the big magnet's position.

components.name: Beam stop (4ID-BS-1)
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.16; the 2021 plan shows it at ~77.6 m, at the downstream wall of 4-ID-H.
components.text: The end of the line: a dense block at the downstream wall of 4-ID-H that safely absorbs whatever beam is left.

enclosures.name: 4-ID-A
enclosures.role: First optics enclosure (FOE): front-end exit table, white-beam slits, HHL mirrors, vertical DCM, collimators, phase-retarder tank, mono shutter
enclosures.notes: Boundaries scaled from the 2021 town-hall 'Sector 4 2024' plan (±0.3 m) and consistent with the PDR 2017 drawing. White/pink-beam enclosure. The 2021 timeline planned optics installation for Apr–Aug 2023 (POLAR town hall 2021). Outer height ≈ 3.4 m, scaled from the 2021 elevation drawing (town hall slide 16, same scale as the metre axis assumed; ±0.3 m). The ratchet wall forms its inboard side; interior width ~1.6 m at the upstream end to ~2.2 m downstream (scaled).

enclosures.name: Shielded transport
enclosures.role: Shielded beam transport: lead-shielded vacuum pipe on the experiment floor (not an enclosure)
enclosures.notes: Existing transport (APS-U PDR 2017; POLAR town hall 2021). An earlier draft called it 'U1-40'; that label is not on the published drawings.

enclosures.name: 4-ID-MH
enclosures.role: Legacy mini-hutch on the transport line
enclosures.notes: Shown on the 2021 'Sector 4 2024' plan. Current contents and function are not documented in the sources found. Outer height ≈ 2.0 m, scaled from the 2021 elevation drawing (town hall slide 16, same scale as the metre axis assumed; ±0.3 m). ~1.2 m wide on the plan (scaled).

enclosures.name: 4-ID-B
enclosures.role: Experimental enclosure (existing, modified): toroid/cylinder focusing mirrors for G/H, diamond window, polarimeter, XBPM, chopper, KB3 and the 2 T electromagnet XMCD station
enclosures.notes: Pre-upgrade '4-ID-B (white/mono beam station)', kept with outboard double doors added (manual + pneumatic). Width ≈2.5 m scaled from the plan (approximate). Tapers at the downstream end (POLAR town hall 2021). Outer height ≈ 3.4 m, scaled from the 2021 elevation drawing (town hall slide 16, same scale as the metre axis assumed; ±0.3 m). Width ≈2.5–2.9 m on the plan; its outboard wall tapers inward at the downstream end. The toroids here serve 4-ID-G and 4-ID-H; beam for G/H passes straight through B.

enclosures.name: 4-ID control room
enclosures.notes: Span re-measured on the 2021 plan: racks at the upstream end level with the 4-ID-B upstream wall (~52.8 m), operator desks at ~60–63.4 m, on the outboard side between 4-ID-B and the existing XTIP control rooms (rooms A/B). The research dossier first estimated 58–68 m (2021 town hall).

enclosures.name: 4-ID-G
enclosures.role: New experimental enclosure: transfocator, KB1, Huber diffractometer (resonant scattering, reflectivity, dichroic imaging)
enclosures.notes: Built during the APS-U dark period (2021 plan: enclosure build-out Sept–Dec 2023, instruments Jan–Apr 2024) on the floor area of the demolished 4-ID-D and the closed 4-ID-C. Double door on the outboard side. Detector-arm sweep radius ~2 m drawn on the plan. Width ≈4.6 m scaled (approximate) (POLAR town hall 2021). Outer height ≈ 4.2 m, scaled from the 2021 elevation drawing (town hall slide 16, same scale as the metre axis assumed; ±0.3 m).

enclosures.name: 4-ID-H
enclosures.role: New experimental enclosure: KB2, 9-1-1 T magnet with DAC/Raman, 4 T magnet, beam stop
enclosures.notes: Double doors on the outboard side and at the downstream inboard corner. Platform and stairs for top-loading the magnet insert, plus an LHe dewar position. The outboard wall angles inward at the downstream end. The PDR (2017) called for a 6 m ceiling for vertical sample loading; the as-built height is not confirmed (POLAR town hall 2021; APS-U PDR 2017). Outer height ≈ 6.2 m, scaled from the 2021 elevation drawing (town hall slide 16, same scale as the metre axis assumed; ±0.3 m). The ~6.2 m drawn height matches the PDR's request for a 6 m ceiling.

instruments.name: Phase-retarder polarization control system
instruments.text: The polarization control on which every POLAR experiment depends. Three plate stages, two of diamond and one of thin silicon for the lowest energies, act as X-ray quarter-wave plates in transmission, with the plane of reflection at 45° to the polarization. Their angles track the monochromator and undulators as the energy changes, and piezo modulation with lock-in detection reads out the small dichroism. They give left or right circular polarization (about 98%) or, with two plates, vertical linear polarization, over about 2.7–14 keV, and are planned to stay as a backup once a polarizing undulator is commissioned.

instruments.name: 2 T electromagnet XMCD station
instruments.text: A quick-switching, water-cooled electromagnet inherited from the old beamline, for magnetic absorption spectroscopy on films, crystals, powders and lightly compressed samples. Adjustable Kirkpatrick–Baez mirrors focus the beam, and photodiodes measure transmission or fluorescence while the field is reversed. Its design range is below 1 megabar, above 10 K and about 0.8 T with a diamond cell. It is configured in the control software but not listed as an end station in the 2026 directory, so its place in the user program is unconfirmed.

instruments.name: Huber diffractometer with 2 T HTS magnet (resonant scattering, reflectivity, spectroscopy)
instruments.text: A multi-axis diffractometer that turns crystals and films to catch magnetic X-ray reflections, with a 2-tesla magnet around the sample. Its split detector arm carries a pixel detector at 0.5–2 m and a polarization analyzer with an avalanche photodiode, and a fluorescence detector looks in from the side. Samples can be cooled to 4 K or heated to 450 K, held in mini diamond cells, strained or put under voltage. An in-vacuum option reaches down to 2.75 keV for magnetic circular dichroism and resonant reflectivity at the L edges of 4d metals.

instruments.name: Dichroic coherent-imaging setup (ptychography, tomography, Bragg CDI)
instruments.text: This setup swaps the diffractometer's cradle for an ultra-stable stack, an air-bearing rotation topped by a nanopositioner, to make 2D and 3D magnetic images at the nanoscale. Mirrors 100 mm from the focus deliver a coherent beam of about 100 nm, and interferometers register the sample position. Detectors are planned at 2.7, 4 and 10 m for forward ptychography, and at 2 m for Bragg coherent diffraction imaging. The 3D method was developed under a 2021 Argonne internal research grant; which modes are offered to general users in 2026 is not confirmed.
sampleEnvironments: room temperature or small electromagnet (others under development)

instruments.name: 9-1-1 T magnet + DAC extreme-conditions spectroscopy instrument
instruments.text: The extreme corner of POLAR: crushing pressure, near-absolute-zero cold and an intense magnetic field at once. A copper–beryllium diamond anvil cell with gas membranes sits on a nanopositioner inside the 9-1-1 T vector magnet, at 1.4–300 K, with Kirkpatrick–Baez mirrors focusing from 600 mm away. Interferometers track drift, a ruby and Raman system reads the pressure, a seven-element detector collects fluorescence through a side window, and a downstream window allows diffraction. Circular dichroism is measured at up to 9 T along the beam and linear dichroism at 1 T across it; the directory lists 3 megabars and 8.7 T for this instrument.
sampleEnvironments: diamond anvil cell with He membranes (3 Mbar operational, 6 Mbar goal)

instruments.name: 4 T cryogen-free magnet
instruments.text: An older, refrigerator-cooled 4-tesla magnet with a small bore at the end of the line, inherited from 4-ID-D. It is reached in 'beam-pass' mode, with the 9-1-1 T magnet moved aside, and uses the broader beam focused by the toroidal mirrors.

instruments.name: MagXES spectrometer (planned)
instruments.text: A planned instrument for magnetic X-ray emission spectroscopy, which reads local magnetism from the X-rays a sample emits, at low temperature, high pressure and high field. It is funded by a 2024 US Department of Energy Early Career award to G. Fabbris; its design, location within POLAR and schedule have not been published.

geometryNotes:
POLAR uses one straight, non-canted line from the 4-ID straight, with two collinear planar undulators separated by a phase shifter. Before the upgrade, sector 4 was canted, feeding soft-x-ray 4-ID-C (CPU undulator) and 4-ID-E/XTIP plus hard-x-ray 4-ID-D. Those branches are gone, and POLAR uses the whole straight (APS News 2020; POLAR town hall 2021; Srajer 2002).

Beam offsets along the line, all small for a 3D model: (1) The HHL mirror pair deflects horizontally (3 mrad grazing angle each) and returns the beam parallel with ~4 mm lateral offset; the direction (inboard/outboard) is not published. (2) The vertical DCM has a fixed 15.6 mm vertical offset, assumed upward. (3) The phase plates transmit the beam straight through, with each plate's diffraction plane tilted 45° about the beam. (4) The M3/M4 toroid/cylinder pair (53.7/54.5 m) deflects horizontally (2–4 mrad grazing angle each) and returns the beam parallel with a few-mm offset. The pair retracts for KB/CRL modes, so the downstream beam axis differs slightly between toroid and KB modes. (5) Each KB pair has the VFM upstream of the HFM, at 3 mrad each.

Enclosures (scaled from the 2021 'Sector 4 2024' plan, ±0.3 m): 4-ID-A 24.4–36.1 m (inside the hall, against the ratchet wall); shielded transport 36.1–50.5 m; mini-hutch 4-ID-MH 50.5–52.8 m; 4-ID-B 52.8–63.3 m (~2.5 m wide, existing, tapered at its downstream end); 4-ID-G 63.5–70.0 m and 4-ID-H 70.0–77.7 m (both new, ~4.6 m wide, H's outboard wall angled inward at the downstream end). All are on the experiment-hall floor (no long-beamline building).

The control room sits on the outboard side alongside B (2021 plan: racks level with B's upstream wall, desks at ~60–63 m), next to the existing XTIP rooms. Outboard double doors on B, G and H; an extra double door at H's downstream inboard corner; a staircase and loading platform beside the 9-1-1 magnet; the 9-1-1 magnet translates inboard for beam-pass. The neighbouring 5-BM hutches lie on the inboard side.

The hutch names changed during design: in the PDR (2017) the instruments were in 4-ID-B and 4-ID-D; in the FDR (2019) the SOE was 4-ID-E and the instruments were in 4-ID-B (diffractometer at 61.3 m) and 4-ID-G (magnet at 73.3 m); as built (2021 design onward) the diffractometer is in new 4-ID-G at ~67.2 m and the magnet in new 4-ID-H at 73.3 m (APS-U FDR 2019; APS-U PDR 2017; POLAR town hall 2021).

Schematic hints for the unpublished offset directions: the 2021 town-hall layout cartoon (slide 16) draws the DCM with the beam stepping up between the crystals (upward offset) and the M1/M2 pair stepping the beam toward the ring (inboard). It is a cartoon, not an engineering drawing.

Hutch heights scaled from the 2021 elevation (slide 16): 4-ID-A and 4-ID-B ≈ 3.4 m, 4-ID-MH ≈ 2.0 m, 4-ID-G ≈ 4.2 m, 4-ID-H ≈ 6.2 m; beam height ≈ 1.4 m above the floor (all ±0.3 m).

The exhibit uses one straight beam axis. The 4 mm (HHL mirrors), 15.6 mm (DCM) and few-mm (toroid) offsets are too small to see at hall scale and are not drawn, but the mirrors are mounted the way the cartoon implies (M1 outboard of the beam, deflecting inboard). Positions follow the 2021 plan where it differs from the FDR table (DCM 30.6 m, phase retarders 33.45 m).

Drawing liberties, for legibility: hutches are cut-away glass rooms whose near wall and roof are left out; the phase-retarder plates are drawn about 7× real size in an open-topped tank, with the 45° roll of their diffraction plane drawn at 225° (optically the same); the 9-1-1 T cryostat is see-through and its 9 T split pair has a wedge cut away to show the DAC; the DAC anvils are drawn ~2× size; the imaging stack is parked on a cart beside the diffractometer; the detector arm is shown at 2θ = 60°/35°; the polarization arrows along the beam have a 0.32 m period and slowed helicity flips.

interactiveIdeas.title: Make it twist: the diamond quarter-wave plate
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors turn a dial that tilts a virtual diamond plate a few tens of arcseconds off its Bragg angle. Two arrows (σ and π components, set at 45°) slip out of step, and the output field traces a line, then an ellipse, then a circle; crossing zero offset reverses the handedness. A 'flip' button wiggles the piezo at 15 Hz and the corkscrew alternates. An energy slider shows the needed offset shrinking at higher energy, until above ~14 keV the plate stops working well.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How a perfect crystal changes linear into circular polarization, why helicity can be flipped mechanically, and why POLAR wants a polarizing undulator for 14–27 keV.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Bragg-transmission phase retarder: δ(Δθ) = (π/2)·Δθq/Δθ, with quarter-wave offset Δθq = 2·t·cosθB·r_e²·λ³·Re(F_h·F_h̄)/(π²·V²) (form used in APS-4ID-POLAR's Pharet calculator). Example computed here: C(111), t = 500 µm, 10 keV (θB = 17.5°, |F|² = 32 f², f_C ≈ 3.0, V = 45.4 Å³) gives Δθq ≈ 2×10⁻⁴ rad ≈ 42″. Pc = sin δ; ±Δθ gives opposite helicity. Two plates (δ = π) give linear-V. The degree of circular polarization degrades when angular divergence and the mono bandwidth (ΔE/E ≈ 1.4×10⁻⁴ maps to Δθ = tanθB·ΔE/E) are not ≪ Δθ. Transmission falls by ×5–30 over 2.8–14 keV, and LCP/RCP intensities differ by 5–30% (Haskel 2018; APS-U PDR 2017). The plate's scattering plane must be at 45° to the incident polarization.

interactiveIdeas.title: The magnetic handshake: XMCD at an absorption edge
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors pick an element (Fe K, Gd L3, Ir L3, U M5) and a magnetized sample. Two absorption curves for left and right helicity appear; their difference reveals the magnet. Flipping the magnetic field (or helicity) inverts the difference. A noise slider shows why 15 Hz switching with lock-in detection beats slow scans.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Element-specific magnetism, why the energy must be tuned to an edge, and how scientists dig sub-percent signals out of noise.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: μ± = μ0·(1 ± Pc·cosφ·A(E)), where φ is the angle between helicity and magnetization. Hard-x-ray XMCD amplitudes are 0.1–6% of the edge jump (Haskel et al. 2007); POLAR's design goal was down to ~10 ppm (APS-U PDR 2017). Sum rules at L2,3: m_orb ∝ ∫(ΔμL3 + ΔμL2), m_spin + 7⟨T_z⟩ ∝ ∫ΔμL3 − 2∫ΔμL2 (Thole et al. 1992). Artefact check: a 0.1 µrad beam-angle change at 8 keV shifts Si(111) energy by ~3 meV (APS-U PDR 2017), so the polarization should be switched at every energy point. Real edge energies: Fe K 7.112, Gd L3 7.243, Ir L3 11.215, U M5 3.552 keV (X-ray Data Booklet).

interactiveIdeas.title: Squeeze it: beam size vs pressure in a diamond anvil cell
interactiveIdeas.concept: A two-diamond press with a culet-size slider. As the visitor shrinks the tips, the pressure gauge climbs (100 GPa = 1 Mbar ≈ 0.6 eV/Å³, since 1 eV/Å³ ≈ 160 GPa; ~3.6 Mbar at Earth's centre), but the sample shrinks too. Overlaid beams compare the old ~15 µm spot, which spills onto the metal gasket, with POLAR's 0.3 µm spot, which fits. Toggling perforated anvils shows how much more X-ray light gets through.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why 'smaller beam = higher pressure', how POLAR extends the pressure range about tenfold, and why hard X-rays are needed to see through diamond.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: P = F/A, so the reachable P rises steeply as culet diameter falls. Perforated anvils need ~2× smaller culets for the same pressure (APS-U PDR 2017). 3–4 Mbar requires ~1 µm beams (APS-U PDR 2017); the PDR (2017) treats 6–7 Mbar as the practical limit of static compression (APS-U PDR 2017); double-stage cells have claimed higher (~1 TPa, Dubrovinskaia et al. 2016, cited in POLAR town hall 2021), but on tiny samples and with debated pressure calibration. Transmission T = exp(−μL): a 100 µm diamond attenuates soft X-rays enormously (Haskel et al. 2007 quote >10¹² for 0.5–1.5 keV; NIST data give ~5×10¹⁰ at 1.5 keV and ~10³⁴ at 1 keV), while a 1 mm diamond attenuates Fe K-edge (7.1 keV) X-rays only ~10× (Haskel et al. 2007; NIST attenuation tables). Partially perforated anvils leave ~0.1–0.2 mm of diamond (Haskel et al. 2007). Pressure is read with ruby (<100 GPa) or the diamond Raman edge (>100 GPa) (POLAR town hall 2021).

interactiveIdeas.title: Edge finder: which elements can POLAR 'talk' to?
interactiveIdeas.concept: An interactive periodic table. Clicking an element shows its K, L or M edges inside 2.7–27 keV and which polarization tool works there: phase plates at 2.7–14 keV; no circular polarization above ~14 keV until a polarizing undulator such as SCAPE arrives (and then elliptical, Pc ~75–90%, in the higher harmonics); the SiC crystals near 2.8 keV. It highlights the rare-earth L3 edges (5.5–9.2 keV; L2 up to 10.3 keV), 5d L3 edges (9.6–11.9 keV; L2 up to 13.7 keV), actinide M4,5 edges (3.3–4 keV) and actinide L2,3 edges (16.3–22.3 keV).
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Resonant X-ray techniques are element-specific; the energy window determines which science is possible.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Use tabulated edges (X-ray Data Booklet), e.g. Ru L3 2.838, Pd L3 3.173, U M4 3.728, Ce L3 5.723, Gd L3 7.243, Yb L3 8.944, Ir L3 11.215, Pt L3 11.564, U L3 17.166, Pu L3 18.057, Ru K 22.117 keV. Undulator: E1 [keV] = 0.950·E²[GeV]/(λu[cm]·(1 + K²/2)) gives ≈ 2.57 keV at K = 2.62 (the ID table lists 2.56 keV), λu = 3 cm, 6 GeV. Higher energies come from odd harmonics.

interactiveIdeas.title: The 45-degree trap: why POLAR needs silicon carbide crystals
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors rotate a monochromator crystal. A polarization-factor meter shows the π (in-plane) component reflected falling to zero as the Bragg angle passes 45° (Si(111) at ~2.8 keV). Swapping to 6H-SiC(0006) moves the angle to 61.4° and the light survives.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Crystals act as polarizers near 45°, a key design constraint for measuring 4d metals (Ru, Rh, Pd) with polarized light.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Kinematic polarization factor: σ → 1, π → |cos2θB|. Dynamical π Darwin width scales with |cos2θB|. Si(111) d = 3.1356 Å gives θB = 45° at 2.796 keV. 6H-SiC(0006) d = 2.522 Å gives θB = 61.4° at 2.8 keV. SiC(0006) Darwin width ~0.29 eV, peak reflectivity ~74% at 2.8 keV (APS-U PDR 2017; Strempfer et al. 2022; POLAR town hall 2021). This matters for source-generated L-V or circular light. For phase-plate polarization, which is generated after the mono, it matters only through the vertical DCM keeping the source's linear-H as σ.

interactiveIdeas.title: Lens-less magnetic camera: dichroic ptychography
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors scan a coherent spot across a hidden pattern of magnetic domains. Each position gives a speckle pattern; pressing 'reconstruct' runs a toy iterative algorithm. Images taken with left and right helicity are subtracted to reveal the domains. A coherence slider (old APS vs APS-U) shows the reconstruction failing without coherence.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why coherence (laser-like light) from APS-U enables imaging finer than the beam itself, and how circular dichroism adds magnetic contrast.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Overlap ≥60% between scan positions. Resolution ≈ λ·z/(N·p), limited by detector NA and dose, not beam size. Coherent fraction per plane ≈ (λ/4π)/(Σ·Σ'). APS-U gives ~200× gain at 10 keV (POLAR workshop slides 2023). POLAR coherent flux is 1.6×10¹² ph/s in 200 nm (Strempfer et al. 2022). The magnetic contrast is the difference of complex transmission for ±helicity; for 3D vector tomography, at least two rotation axes are needed (Donnelly et al. 2017).

interactiveIdeas.title: Polarization switching race
interactiveIdeas.concept: A timeline game comparing ways to flip X-ray helicity: the 2002-era soft-x-ray CPU (~5 minutes), diamond phase plates on a piezo (~13–40 Hz), SCAPE orbit bumps (≥10 Hz planned) and the X-undulator (1–5 Hz). Visitors see how slow switching lets drifts masquerade as magnetic signals.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Measurement design: modulate the thing you want to measure faster than everything that drifts.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: CPU ~5 min helicity switch in 2002 (Srajer 2002). Phase plates 12.7–15 Hz typical (Haskel et al. 2007; POLAR town hall 2021), up to 40 Hz reported (Srajer 2002). SCAPE orbit-bump scheme: ~30 µrad bumps, ≥95% polarization purity, 10 Hz design (APS-U PDR 2017; POLAR town hall 2021). X-undulator: 7.5 mm quarter-period motion at 1 Hz, or 5 Hz with dual-XU detuning (Qian et al. 2024).

funFacts: POLAR flips the 'handedness' of its X-rays by rocking a thin diamond with a piezo actuator: about 15 times per second in the 2021 design (POLAR town hall 2021), and 12.7 Hz in the 2007 high-pressure instrument (Haskel et al. 2007).
In 2002, switching the helicity of sector 4's soft-x-ray circularly polarizing undulator took about 5 minutes (Srajer 2002).
The 9-1-1 T magnet is deliberately cooled with liquid helium instead of a cryogen-free cryocooler, because a cryocooler's vibrations would blur a 300 nm beam (Strempfer et al. 2022).

Diamond is nearly transparent to POLAR's hard X-rays: 1 mm of diamond dims the beam only ~10× at the iron edge (7.1 keV), while just 0.1 mm stops soft X-rays almost completely (by ~5×10¹⁰ at 1.5 keV and ~10³⁴ at 1 keV) (Haskel et al. 2007; NIST attenuation tables).
Before the upgrade, POLAR's predecessor 4-ID-D was described as the only hard-x-ray XMCD beamline in the US and was oversubscribed 3–4× (APS-U PDR 2017).
POLAR's goal pressure, ~6 Mbar, is about 1.6 times the pressure at the centre of the Earth (~3.6 Mbar) (POLAR town hall 2021; PREM, Dziewonski & Anderson 1981).

A wobble of just 0.1 microradian in the X-ray source shifts the monochromator energy by ~3 meV at 8 keV, enough to fake a magnetic signal if the polarization is not switched at every energy point (APS-U PDR 2017).

The two undulators together would radiate about 20.6 kW at their 9.0 mm design minimum gap, close to the 21 kW limit of the high-heat-load front end; users are limited to gaps of ≥9.1–9.4 mm (APS ID table, Sep 2026; APS-U FDR 2019, ch. 3).

POLAR's hutches were renamed twice during design. The experiments moved from '4-ID-B/4-ID-D' (2017) to '4-ID-B/4-ID-G' (2019) to the built '4-ID-G/4-ID-H' (APS-U PDR 2017; APS-U FDR 2019; POLAR town hall 2021).
POLAR was selected for the APS-U scope in July 2016, after a proposal by a team of 15 scientists from US universities and national labs (POLAR town hall 2021; Haskel CV 2024).
The first scientists to use POLAR, in the January–May 2025 run, came from the University of Wisconsin to study flexomagnetism, which is magnetism created by bending (APS News, Jun 2025).
Planned ptychography detector distances reach 10 m, longer than the 4-ID-G hutch itself (POLAR workshop slides 2023).
XMCD was first observed in 1987 at the iron K edge, a hard-x-ray absorption edge of the same kind POLAR uses every day (Schütz et al. 1987).
POLAR's First Experiments Workshop on 28 June 2023 was the first in the APS-U series of feature-beamline 'first experiments' workshops (APS News, Apr 2023).

openQuestions: As-built component positions in 4-ID-B/G/H are not published in a table. The diffractometer (67.2 m) and magnet (73.3 m) positions come from the 2021 town-hall slides and plan. Positions of the B-table components (window, polarimeter, XBPM, chopper, KB3) and of KB1 and KB2 are inferred from the FDR order and scaled from the plan drawing (±0.5 m).

The FDR (2019) put the diffractometer at 61.3 m in an enlarged 4-ID-B and the toroids at 48 and 50 m in a new 4-ID-E. The 2021 redesign moved the toroids to 53.7/54.5 m and the instruments into new 4-ID-G/H. We could not confirm that the as-built layout matches the 2021 plan in every detail.

Source upgrade: the FDR planned two in-line SCAPE devices after the project, and the town hall timeline put the replacement around 2026. The Sep 2026 ID table still shows planar APS30#4/#9. A 2023 Argonne internal research grant (LDRD) funded a permanent-magnet 'X-undulator' for POLAR. Which device (if any) will be installed, and when, is unknown. Both need a small round vacuum chamber instead of the standard 6.3 × 16 mm elliptical APS-U insertion-device vacuum chamber.
The APS30 devices are pre-upgrade magnet structures (the IPAC'24 undulator table lists the 3.0 cm period only among 'Existing IDs'); whether and how they were refurbished is not stated.
Directions of the lateral beam offsets: white-beam mirror pair ~4 mm and toroid pair a few mm horizontally (inboard or outboard?); DCM 15.6 mm vertical offset (assumed upward).
Phase-plate details at POLAR (diamond thicknesses, which plates are in pr1/pr2, actual modulation frequency in user mode) are not published. The 15 Hz figure comes from 2021 planning slides.
The status of the 4-ID-B 2 T electromagnet station in user operation is unclear: it is configured in Bluesky but not listed as an endstation in the beamline directory.
Achieved pressure (directory: 3 Mbar) vs the 6 Mbar design goal; magnet field with DAC (directory 8.7 T vs 9 T spec); 9-1-1 bore quoted as 74 mm (VTI, SRI 2022) vs 3 inches (7.5 cm, slides).

Whether dichroic ptychography/tomography is offered in general user mode (the directory lists 'dichroic imaging, 400 nm resolution' and 'dichroic ptychography' as techniques). Where the 4 m and 10 m ptychography detectors physically sit (possibly in 4-ID-H).
Contents and purpose of the legacy mini-hutch 4-ID-MH (50.5–52.8 m), and the hutch ceiling heights (PDR asked for 6 m at the magnet hutch).

Fate of the former soft-x-ray programs: 4-ID-C closed April 2021 (planned), and 4-ID-E (XTIP SX-STM) lost its source when the canted straight was converted. A 2025 APS photo shows soft-x-ray XMCD by the former 4-ID-C scientist at 29-ID, but no official relocation statement was found.
MagXES instrument design, location within POLAR and schedule are unknown.
The identity of the first POLAR user group (UW–Madison, flexomagnetism) is from APS news; linking it to the Kawasaki group's GdAuGe work is our inference.
Is there a dedicated beam stop or shutter at the 4-ID-G/4-ID-H boundary (needed for H access while G runs)? Added here as an inferred shutter at ~69.7 m.
Are the 6H-SiC(0006) crystals installed in the CINEL DCM and used in 2026? They matter only for source-generated polarization near 2.8 keV.
